# Where the platform runs things

This service is the register of the places the platform serves from. It answers
two questions and no others: what places exist, and which of them a given
service is offered at for the project asking.

It runs nothing and provisions nothing. Nothing here starts, stops, moves or
resizes anything a customer owns.

## A place (Location)

`locations.miloapis.com/v1alpha1 Location` is one place the platform serves
traffic or runs work from. A place is usually a city, not a cloud vendor's
region: `us-east-1` and `dfw` are the kind of names that appear.

Names are exact and are the only handle that works. Anything that has to say
where something should run names a place by `metadata.name`, spelled exactly as
this service spells it. A name that is not on the list for a service can never
be satisfied — a request that uses one waits, unplaced, instead of failing
loudly — so take names verbatim from `locations_list` rather than inferring
them from a city, an airport code, or a name that worked in another project.

## What a place declares about itself: topology

`spec.topology` is a map of keys to values describing where the place is. It is
open-ended, and new keys can appear without anything else changing. The keys
seen most often:

- `topology.datum.net/city-code` — the city, as a short code, e.g. `IAD`,
  `DFW`, `LHR`. Reported separately as `cityCode` by both tools, because most
  questions about where something runs are really questions about which city.
- `topology.datum.net/region` — a broader grouping the place belongs to, e.g.
  `us-east-1`.

Topology is what selectors match on. When someone wants "every place in
Dallas", or "everywhere in a region", the thing being matched is exactly these
key/value pairs, so read them off `locations_list` before writing a selector
rather than guessing which keys exist.

`spec.coordinates` is where the place sits on a map, in decimal degrees, when
it has been recorded. `locations_get` returns it; use it for distance and
geography questions, never for placement, which goes by name or by topology.

## Two different questions: offered, and serving

These are separate and both matter.

**Offered** — whether a named service is available to this project at a place.
It is recorded per (service, place) pair, and it is what `locations_list`
filters on: the list holds only the places where the named service really is
offered to the project that asked. A place absent from the list means one of
two things — the service is not offered there at all, or this project is not
entitled to it there — and in both cases the answer is the same: it cannot be
used, and asking for it will not make it work.

**Serving** — whether the place itself is up and taking work right now,
reported as `ready`. A place can be offered and not ready: it is a real place
the project may use, but nothing will start there until it recovers.

So the useful reading is:

- offered and `ready: true` — usable now.
- offered and `ready: false` — a real choice, but not right now. Worth saying
  out loud before promising anything will start there. Somewhere else may be
  the better answer today.
- not on the list at all — not a choice. Do not suggest it, and do not write it
  into anything.

`locations_get` adds `readyReason` and `readyMessage` for a place that is not
serving. Both empty means nothing has been reported either way, which is not
the same as a reported failure: it means the answer is not yet known, so say
that rather than describing it as broken.

## Choosing a place

1. Call `locations_list` with the service, e.g. `compute`. The project is taken
   from the request, never from an argument, so there is nothing to pass and
   nothing to guess.
2. Prefer a place that is offered and serving.
3. Narrow by what the person actually asked for — a city, a region, closeness
   to their users — using `cityCode` and `topology`, and `coordinates` from
   `locations_get` when the question is about distance.
4. Use the name verbatim.

An empty list is a real answer, not a failure: the service is offered nowhere
this project can use. Say so plainly, and say that it is the current answer
rather than a lookup that went wrong.

A refusal is not an empty list. If either tool reports that the records
answering the question are missing, nothing was actually looked at. Do not
report that as "no places" — say the question could not be asked, repeat which
record was missing, and make clear the person who asked did nothing wrong.

## What these tools cannot do

Both tools are read-only. There is no tool here that adds a place, changes one,
takes one out of service, or moves work between places. If someone wants any of
that, the answer is who to ask, not an attempt.
